origin.audio: Last night at the book club, Sara summarised chapter six. In it, the plot turns when Mara finds her grandmother's letter hidden inside an old book, and the pacing slows to let us feel her hesitation. Sara found it deeply moving, although she admitted the ending is a little predictable. Tom disagreed politely: he said he could not relate to Mara at all, because he has never waited anxiously for news from anyone.

prompt.es: Escucha otra vez y elige qué matiz tiene la opinión de Sara sobre el capítulo.

choices.text: Positive, with one small reservation.
Enthusiastic, without any reservation at all.
Negative, despite a few good points.

feedback.es: Sara lo encuentra muy conmovedor pero admite que el final es algo previsible: aprecio con una pequeña reserva.

origin.text: I see your point, Tom, but I would ___ issue with the idea that the ending is rushed: the clues were planted in chapter two.

prompt.es: Escribe tu intervención en el club de lectura: resumen, recuerdo y respuesta.

answer.text: Thanks, Tom. I see your point, but I would take issue with the claim that the ending was rushed. In chapter six, the plot turns when Mara finds her grandmother's old letter hidden in an old book, and the pacing slows so that we can feel her hesitation. Although the final pages are quiet, I found them very moving. I can relate to Mara, because I remember waiting for a letter from my own grandmother every summer. I will never forget opening the envelope and seeing her small, careful handwriting. That memory made the last scene feel true to me, and it is bound to strike a chord with anyone who has waited for news. Perhaps the ending is not exciting, but it is honest. I also regret not keeping her letters, which may be why the chapter reminds me of her so strongly. What do the rest of you think?
accepted: Thanks, Tom. I see your point, but I would take issue with the claim that the ending was rushed. In chapter six, the plot turns when Mara finds her grandmother's old letter hidden in an old book, and the pacing slows so that we can feel her hesitation. Although the final pages are quiet, I found them very moving. I can relate to Mara, because I remember waiting for a letter from my own grandmother every summer. I will never forget opening the envelope and seeing her small, careful handwriting. That memory made the last scene feel true to me, and it is bound to strike a chord with anyone who has waited for news. Perhaps the ending is not exciting, but it is honest. I also regret not keeping her letters, which may be why the chapter reminds me of her so strongly. What do the rest of you think?

I understand your point, Tom, but I do not agree that the ending was rushed, and I would take issue with calling it boring. In this chapter, the plot changes when Mara finds a letter in her aunt's kitchen and decides to read it in secret, and the pacing slows to show how nervous she is. Though the last scene is slow, I thought it was gripping. I can relate to Mara, because I remember writing letters to my cousin every summer when I was a child. I will never forget waiting by the gate for his reply, and that memory reminds me how important small moments can be. It is bound to strike a chord with many readers, even if the ending is not exciting. I regret not finishing the book earlier, because I would love to discuss it with the whole club. Does anyone else feel the same way?

feedback.es: Una buena intervención resume el capítulo, conecta con un recuerdo vivido y responde con cortesía a la otra opinión.

origin.audio: Some members argued that the novel is overrated, and Carlos admitted that he found the middle slow. Even so, he said he would recommend it, because it makes you think about your own family long after you have finished the last page.
